newsitem.title: FRANCE: EMU abcess lingers after Jospin maiden speech.
newsitem.headline: EMU abcess lingers after Jospin maiden speech.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's first speech to parliament has left serious questions over the state of France's public finances and the future of Europe's economic and monetary union.
He delivered an expected message on Thursday -- that his new left-wing government was committed to launching a single European currency on time in 1999.
But it came with the qualifier that he had only just started a campaign to balance financial rectitude with the need for more solidarity and jobs in Europe.

And perhaps most importantly, it said nothing about France's will or ability to limit its public deficit which stood at 4.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996, to the three percent goal set by the Maastricht treaty for joining the euro launch.

Speculation has been rife for several months that France's public deficit this year could hit anything up to 3.8 percent of GDP because of lacklustre economic growth, weak tax revenues and a social security deficit considerably larger than forecast.
Jospin argues that a deficit approaching 3.0 per cent is close enough under the terms of the Maastricht treaty.

But economists say the question now is whether France will even get close. Jospin would have a harder time pleading his case the closer the deficit gets to 3.5 percent, and the overrun could be even bigger, they say.

That could go down badly with Germany, where the powerful central bank and a public uneasy about losing the strong German mark are both pressing for the three percent goal be respected right down to the very last decimal point.
Even if Bonn may be forced to relax its stance due to budget troubles of its own, analysts believe leeway is limited.

The true state of French finances will take a little time to emerge. Jospin ordered an audit of public finances to finish by mid-July. He limited himself on Thursday to saying first signs were that "the situation of public finances is serious."

Reactions in the wake of his speech were varied, with some economists saying his comment on the state of public finances was probably designed to warn voters his hands were tied on spending and that he has in any case signed up to the euro.

"I feel comfortable with my initial assumption that this government is not going to add to the deficit. I heard nothing in the speech to change that," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, Paris economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

Her prediction is the deficit this year will be 3.2 to 3.5 percent. "3.5 percent is the cut-off point for the Germans. I think markets can live with anything up to 3.5. But anything over that will be seriously bad news for the EMU bulls."
Others felt Jospin had made spending commitments which, if limited, showed belt-tightening was no longer the priority.

"He actually announced potentially a lot of spending," said ABN Amro's Philippe Brossard. "He (Jospin) pushed up allowances for housing and he pushed up the back-to-school allowance. He's talking about cutting value-added tax and more public works."

"Tensions will remain because it sounded like the deficit is going to be 3.3-3.4 (percent). The Germans are going to start screaming that they're not doing the right thing and that they should be trying to get to three percent," he said.
"But in Germany the situation is hard as well, I don't see any way of them getting to three percent."
In some ways, Jospin appeared to have taken a relatively modest tack on the spending front.

He said the minimum wage would rise by four percent, seen by many economists as a "reasonable" compromise at the lower end of the hikes requested by union's and his Communist partners in the "Pink-Green-Red" coalition.

The cost of raising the minimum wage was estimated by one economist at about six billion francs. Another said the important point was that this sent a signal that any rises would have to be moderate elsewhere, notably in a public sector which employs about one in four French workers.
Less expected was a quadrupling of a "back-to-school" pay out for those with children in education, which economists estimated would cost seven to 10 billion francs, and further housing aid.

A cut in VAT on basic goods like bread and milk -- Jospin made no commitment in his speech but spoke of a cut to five percent from 5.5 in his election campaign -- would add five billion to the bill in foregone revenue, economists say.
"This is worrying," said Eric Chaney, Paris-based economist at U.S. bank Morgan Stanley. "One cannot say that France is on a trend (towards the three percent deficit target).
While some said Jospin was wise to wait for the financial audit before a mini-budget in the autumn, Chaney said this only put off the agony and would leave little time to rectify French finances.
